analysis.one_liner: Bans medical debt from ever appearing on consumer credit reports.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 63 House cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal credit law so that medical bills could never appear on a person's credit report, even after being sent to a collection agency. It would also order the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to write rules barring lenders from considering medical debt when deciding whether to make a loan. It was introduced by Rep. Katie Porter with dozens of Democratic cosponsors, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or action of any kind.
analysis.who_benefits: The large share of American households carrying medical debt — including many with insurance — would benefit. Medical bills in collections would no longer appear on credit reports, protecting their credit scores, lowering their cost of borrowing, and making it easier to rent an apartment, buy a car, or get a job or mortgage without a medical bill standing in the way.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The roughly 100 million Americans with medical debt

how_it_helps.text: It adds an exclusion to the Fair Credit Reporting Act barring any adverse medical-debt information — including medical debt placed for collection or charged off — from consumer credit reports.
It requires the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, within one year, to change its rules so creditors cannot obtain or use medical debt information when deciding whether to extend credit.

It defines medical debt broadly to cover any debt arising in whole or in part from the receipt of medical services, products, or devices, so the protection reaches bills from hospitals, doctors, pharmacies, and medical equipment alike.

analysis.who_pays: Credit bureaus, debt collection agencies, and some lenders lose a source of information and leverage: collection agencies lose the threat of credit damage as a tool to push people to pay medical bills, and lenders lose medical debt data when judging borrowers. Some unpaid medical costs may also end up shifted back to hospitals and insurers in the form of harder-to-collect bills.

drawbacks.text: Lenders argue medical debt is a legitimate indicator of unpaid obligations, and the bill removes it from their underwriting; that could lead some lenders to raise prices for all borrowers or apply cruder proxies to offset risk they can no longer measure directly.
Shielding medical debt from credit reports does nothing to reduce the underlying bills themselves — people would still owe the money, and hospitals and providers could still sue over unpaid balances.

Federal credit scoring relies heavily on the data credit bureaus report; carving out one debt type raises scoring-accuracy concerns that an honest supporter would have to address, including how the change interacts with mortgage underwriting rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to households are real and direct: medical debt affects tens of millions of Americans, often from emergencies outside their control, and a collections tradeline can depress a credit score for years and block access to housing and affordable credit. The main costs fall on credit bureaus and collection agencies rather than on taxpayers, and the risk that lenders offset lost information with higher prices for everyone is plausible but modest compared with the harm the bill removes. The bill's honest weakness is that it treats the symptom — credit damage — rather than the medical bills themselves.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the week after introduction and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 19, 2023, and referred to the House Financial Services Committee on October 25, 2023.
That referral was the bill's last recorded action; no hearing, markup, or vote followed before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
All 63 House supporters listed on the bill were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored it, and the committee that controlled its fate was chaired by the opposing party.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus, debt collection agencies, and lenders that use medical debt in underwriting are better off, since nothing changed: the threat of credit damage from medical bills remains a tool for collecting unpaid hospital and doctor bills.

sides.party_line_note: All 63 listed sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, including two members generally viewed as moderates; no Republicans signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Consumer credit bureaus and medical debt collection agencies
industries.note: These firms collect and sell medical debt data that lenders and landlords rely on; the bill would remove medical debt from the reports they sell and cut off a key payment-pressure tool.

industries.industry: Consumer lenders, credit card issuers, and mortgage providers
industries.note: The bill would bar lenders from considering medical debt in underwriting decisions, removing one risk signal but also removing a factor that can penalize even financially responsible borrowers who had a health emergency.
